subject: Dedicated reservation options — prewarm & canary playbook for HydraIO
messages:
From: Connor O'Brien <connor.obrien@redwood.ai>

Cc: Marissa Cole <marissa.cole@redwood.ai>, Karthik Iyer <karthik.iyer@redwood.ai>

Subject: Dedicated reservation options — prewarm & canary playbook for HydraIO

Elena — great talking earlier. As promised, attached are three distinct dedicated-reservation pathways tailored to HydraIO's target 99th pct latency and inference throughput goals. High-level summary below; full details are in the PDF and the burn model spreadsheet attached.

We designed options to balance: predictable throughput, cost certainty, and ability to scale quickly during product launches. Each option includes
- cluster footprint (GPUs / node mix),
- minimum-guarantee (floor) you pay for,
- recommended ramp schedule and canary rollout,
- warm / pre-warm approach to reduce cold-start token latency, and
- fallback policies (smaller variants / burst pool) to preserve SLA if capacity constrained.

Option A — Pilot + rapid scale (low initial commit)
- Cluster: 10 x A100-equivalent GPUs (1 node pool)
- Min GPUs: 10 (30-day minimum)
- Ramp: 10 -> 40 over 60 days (triggered by steady-state QPS >= 30% of forecast)
- Canary: 10% traffic on day 0, expand to 50% over 7 days
- Prewarm: 1 prewarm pool (2 GPUs) to keep KV cache warm for hottest prefixes
- Notes: Best if you need fast validation with bounded spend; supports bursts via shared-hosted pool at higher runtime cost.

Option B — Production onramp (balanced)
- Cluster: 50 x A100-equivalent GPUs (multi-rack)
- Min GPUs: 30 (90-day minimum guarantee)
- Ramp: 30 -> 50 over 90 days with weekly checkpoints
- Canary: 5% traffic initially, progressive rollout with automated rollback on quality regressions
- Prewarm: Warm-set preloading of weights, 10% warm standby capacity during peak windows
- Notes: Predictable throughput and unit economics; recommended when aiming for a product milestone (beta -> GA).

Option C — Anchored capacity (SLA-critical)
- Cluster: 150 x A100-equivalent GPUs (reserved lanes + burst pool)
- Min GPUs: 150 (6-month commitment)
- Ramp: Activate 50% on day 1, 100% by month 3, with runway credits for first 30 days
- Canary: Staged canary per-region (us-west/us-east) with automated failover to secondary region
- Prewarm: Full warm standby (20% of capacity) to eliminate cold token latency for critical prefixes
- Notes: Includes SLA credits and a dedicated SRE onboarding window.

Cost framework (estimate; see spreadsheet): per-GPU equivalent committed rate (USD/hr) scales down with size; Pilot has higher per-GPU rate but low absolute spend. Optional warmup credits reduce initial burn for the first 30 days.

Next steps: 1) confirm which option you'd like to horizon against, 2) we’ll schedule a 30-min technical onboarding with our SRE to map IP/caching routes, and 3) legal/Procurement loops in for a term sheet (I included a draft timeline in the PDF).

If helpful, I can also run a quick simulation with your real QPS traces — drop sample traces and I’ll include hit-rate-sensitive burn scenarios.

Thanks,
Connor O'Brien

Elena — great questions. Short answers first, followed by the acceptance-test language you asked for.

1) Minimums & billing: the "Min GPUs" is a billing floor for the reserved contract. You pay for the floor at the committed rate regardless of usage. Burst capacity beyond the floor can be handled either through a dedicated burst pool (at a lower surplus price) or via Redwood's hosted fallback (higher per-token rate). We can structure a partial credit for unused floor in month 1 as a one-time buffer if that helps Procurement.

2) Prewarm billing: warm-standby GPUs are typically included in the committed footprint for Options B and C (i.e., billed at the committed rate). For Option A we propose a small warm pool billed at the same committed rate for the duration of the 30-day pilot. If you prefer, we can convert warm-standby to a cheaper "standby credit" model for months 2–3 (reduces commit but increases per-hour warm activation latency).

3) Cold-start latency: with weight preloading + KV prefix warming we see median cold-start improvements from ~600ms token latency to ~60–120ms for the first tokens on the hot prefixes (numbers depend on model size and batch policy). The attached spreadsheet includes a per-GPU token-per-second profile and an example trace showing expected tail improvements.

4) SLA credits across regions: if a failover triggers cross-region routing, SLA measurement is per-request region. Credits are prorated by impacted region and request volume. We'll include an explicit clause for multi-region failover credits in the term sheet.

Proposed acceptance gates (30/60/90 day):
- Day 30 (Platform Acceptance): Cluster provisioning verified, successful canary at 5% for 7 days, latency <= target median for 90% of test prompts, basic logging and traces in Console enabled.
- Day 60 (Feature Acceptance): Traffic ramp to 50% of target QPS, burst tests to 120% of expected peak for 1 hour with <2% error rate, integration points validated (KMS, VPC peering).
- Day 90 (Operational Acceptance): Reach target throughput for steady-state, SLA measurement engaged, runbook validated via a simulated failover incident with successful rollback criteria.

I'll update the PDF with a short acceptance clause and a version of the burn model that shows the 3 acceptance milestones. Want me to send an updated PDF to Procurement?

Connor
Senior Solutions Architect, Redwood Inference

Attachments: hydraio_dedicated_options_v1.pdf (updated - acceptance gates)
